metadata.title: Claude, Judged.
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Turkish. Wagwan check: charsum('claude-liam-llm-as-a-judge') % 10 == 7, not 0.
metadata.note: deep-explainer, fresh technical build (not sourced from ai1-cli or any single document) covering the 8 required points: test case structure, judge prompts, output parsing, bias mitigation, metric abstraction, batch evaluation runner, aggregation, CI/CD integration. 4 acts, 2 points/act. Content is general, well-established LLM-evaluation engineering practice; the one specific citation (position/verbosity/self-enhancement bias) is Zheng et al. 2023, 'Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena' -- see FACTCHECK.md for the honesty/sourcing method note. No Manim on this machine (pangocairo not installed) -- MANIM lane absorbed into REMOTION, as in the prior two deep-explainer builds. VOX quota: 6 real Wikimedia Commons photographs (public domain / CC0 / CC BY), used as METAPHOR imagery (filing records, a courtroom, a telegraph operator, scales of justice, two WWII aircraft-assembly-line photos) since the topic itself has no historical referent -- captioned as illustrative, never claimed to depict LLM evaluation literally. This is the 16:9 master; a 9:16 Short is derived via runtime/scripts/shorts.py into short/. Both compiled at 4K (16:9: 3840x2160; 9:16: 2160x3840). GATE P: PENDING, see PEDAGOGY.md.

beats.narration_text: Merhaba — this is Liam, in for Bear. Ask five different eval frameworks how they use an LLM as a judge, and you get five different half-built systems — until you look at what they all actually need underneath: eight real components, from the test case to the CI gate. Let's build the whole pipeline, in order.

show.event: composer cold-opens, spark + 'Merhaba, Liam' greeting settles
command types itself in: the eight-components question
send arms, runningText plays
RESULT lines land in sequence

props.command: Walk me through everything a real LLM-as-a-judge evaluation system needs, in order, from the test case to the CI gate.
output: a test case is a structured object, not a chat
the judge's own answer needs bias-checking, not just parsing
the last mile is a CI gate, not a spreadsheet

beats.narration_text: Act one: define the case.

show.event: act card settles: 'I — Define the Case'

beats.narration_text: Every judgment starts with a record, not a conversation. A test case is a structured object: the input prompt, the candidate output being graded, an optional reference answer, and metadata — category, difficulty, the tags a later report will group by.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of index-card / filing-folder records -- illustrative of a structured record, not a literal depiction of LLM evaluation. Already sourced, see media/A1-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push into the filing folders
serif label lands: 'a record, not a conversation'

beats.narration_text: Four layers, always in the same order. Input: what was asked. Candidate: what the model under test actually said. Reference: a gold answer, when one exists. Rubric: the criteria the judge is told to apply. Skip the rubric, and the judge is just guessing what you meant.

show.event: four layers stack in order: Input, Candidate, Reference, Rubric
caption settles: 'skip the rubric, the judge guesses'

layers.title: Candidate
layers.sub: what the model under test said

layers.title: Reference
layers.sub: a gold answer, when one exists

layers.title: Rubric
layers.sub: the criteria the judge is told to apply

props.caption: skip the rubric, the judge guesses

beats.narration_text: Now the judge itself — not a person, a second LLM call, given a role: 'you are an impartial judge.' That framing isn't decoration. It's the first line of a prompt built to resist the same sloppy habits its own model would use on an ordinary chat turn.

shot.prompt: real archival courtroom-gavel photo -- illustrative of the judge role, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A1-3.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push onto the gavel
serif label lands: 'you are an impartial judge'

beats.narration_text: A working judge prompt has four parts on screen: the role framing, the rubric, the candidate output verbatim, and an explicit instruction on how to answer — usually a fixed format, because the next step in this pipeline has to read that answer back out.

show.event: four chips snap in: Role, Rubric, Candidate output, Answer format
caption settles

props.caption: the next step has to read this answer back out

beats.narration_text: One fork happens before any of that: is there a reference answer? Reference-based judging compares the candidate against a known-good answer — narrower, more reliable. Reference-free judging asks the judge to grade on the rubric alone, when no gold answer exists.

show.event: question card settles: 'is there a reference answer?'
two outcome cards land: reference-based / reference-free

branches.label: Reference-free
branches.fix: necessary when no gold answer exists

resolver.label: Both are legal
resolver.detail: the fork decides HOW the rubric gets applied

beats.narration_text: One more habit worth stealing: ask for reasoning before the score, not after. A judge forced to write its justification first, then commit to a verdict, catches its own contradictions — the same way asking a person to explain their answer does.

show.event: chip sequence: Reasoning first, then Verdict
caption settles

props.caption: catches its own contradictions before they're scored

beats.narration_text: Act two: read the verdict.

show.event: act card settles: 'II — Read the Verdict'

beats.narration_text: The judge's answer arrives as text — a sentence, a paragraph, sometimes a stray apology. Somewhere between that raw response and a number in a spreadsheet, someone has to turn language back into data. That step is output parsing, and it breaks more often than any other.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of a telegraph operator -- illustrative of turning a raw signal into structured data, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A2-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push onto the operator at the telegraph
serif label lands: 'language back into data'

beats.narration_text: Two ways to extract the score. Regex over free text — fast to write, and it silently breaks the moment the judge phrases things differently. Constrained output — JSON mode, or a function-call schema — forces the shape at generation time, so parsing becomes a formality.

show.event: two tracks diverge: regex arcs up warn, constrained output arcs down good

beats.narration_text: Even a perfectly parsed verdict can be a wrong one. In 2023, Zheng and colleagues, benchmarking judges for M-T Bench, named the specific ways an LLM judge tilts the scale without anyone asking it to.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of a Scales of Justice statue -- illustrative of fairness/balance, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A2-3.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push onto the scales
serif label lands: 'tilts the scale, unasked'

beats.narration_text: Three documented biases. Position bias: favoring whichever answer it reads first, or last. Verbosity bias: rewarding length over quality. Self-enhancement bias: a model quietly preferring answers written in its own family's voice.

show.event: three chips snap in: Position, Verbosity, Self-enhancement
caption settles with the citation

items: Self-enhancement bias — favors its own family
props.caption: Zheng et al., 2023 — MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena

beats.narration_text: Position bias has a direct fix: run the comparison twice, swapping which answer appears first, and keep only the verdicts that agree both times. Disagreement isn't noise to average away — it's the judge admitting the two answers were closer than the rubric could resolve.

show.event: question card: 'does the order change the verdict?'
two outcomes: agrees both ways / disagrees

data.question: Swap the order — does the verdict change?

branches.label: Disagrees
branches.detail: the answers were closer than the rubric resolved

resolver.label: Run it twice, swapped
resolver.detail: the cheapest bias check that exists

beats.narration_text: None of this makes the judge unbiased. It makes the bias bounded and visible instead of silent — which is the most any single evaluation step can honestly promise.

show.event: spark line breathing beat: 'bounded, not solved'

props.caption: the honest limit of this step

beats.narration_text: Act three: judge at scale.

show.event: act card settles: 'III — Judge at Scale'

beats.narration_text: One test case, once, is a demo. A real evaluation suite runs hundreds or thousands of cases, across every rubric that matters, on every model version that ships. That's not a script anymore — it's a production line, and it needs the same discipline one gets.

shot.prompt: real archival WWII aircraft-assembly-line photo -- illustrative of running many cases at scale, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A3-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow drift along the assembly line
serif label lands: 'a production line, not a script'

beats.narration_text: The fix is an abstraction most harnesses converge on independently: separate WHAT gets measured from HOW it gets scored. A metric is an interface — correctness, helpfulness, safety, groundedness — and any of them can plug into the same judge-calling machinery underneath.

show.event: layers stack: Metric interface, Judge-calling machinery
caption settles

layers.title: Judge-calling machinery
layers.sub: the same underneath, for every metric

props.caption: swap the metric, never the machinery

beats.narration_text: Underneath that interface, the runner's real engineering problems: rate limits on the judge model itself, retries when a call fails or returns garbage, and concurrency — running many cases in parallel without tripping the same limits twice.

show.event: three chips snap in: Rate limits, Retries, Concurrency

items: Rate limits on the judge model
props.caption: the runner's real job

beats.narration_text: One more runner habit that pays for itself immediately: cache the judge's verdict on an identical input. Re-run the same candidate against the same rubric, and a cache hit means zero cost and a guaranteed identical score — not a second roll of an inherently noisy dice.

show.event: two tracks: re-run arcs up warn, cache hit arcs down good

tracks.label: Re-run the judge
tracks.outcome: full cost, and a noisy re-roll

beats.narration_text: At thousands of cases, some calls will fail outright — a timeout, a malformed response the parser can't save. A batch runner that stops on the first failure never finishes; one that logs the failure and keeps going is the only version that actually scales.

show.event: chip reveal: 'stop on failure' struck through, 'log and continue' lands

items: Stop on first failure — never finishes
Log and continue — the only version that scales
props.caption: partial failure is the normal case at scale

beats.narration_text: The payoff of the abstraction shows up here: adding a new rubric — grading for a new kind of safety violation, say — means writing one new metric, not touching the runner, the parser, or the bias-mitigation pass at all.

show.event: one new chip lands beside the untouched pipeline

beats.narration_text: Act four: ship the judgment.

show.event: act card settles: 'IV — Ship the Judgment'

beats.narration_text: A batch of individual verdicts isn't a result yet. Someone has to roll thousands of per-case scores into the handful of numbers a team can actually act on — and then decide what those numbers are allowed to block.

shot.prompt: real archival WWII aircraft-production-line photo -- illustrative of continuous production, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A4-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow drift down the production line
serif label lands: 'a handful of numbers, not a pile'

beats.narration_text: Aggregation turns cases into a report: the mean score across the suite, the pass rate against a threshold, a win rate when two model versions were compared head to head, and a breakdown by category — one weak rubric shouldn't hide inside a healthy average.

show.event: four chips snap in: Mean, Pass rate, Win rate, By-category breakdown

props.caption: one weak rubric shouldn't hide inside the average

beats.narration_text: The number that matters most isn't the score itself — it's the score against the last known-good baseline. A model that scores eighty-five percent is meaningless alone; eighty-five against yesterday's eighty-eight is a regression, and the report has to say so.

show.event: two layers compare: 'This run: 85%' against 'Baseline: 88%'
caption settles: 'a regression, and the report says so'

props.caption: a regression, and the report has to say so

beats.narration_text: Wire that comparison into the build, and the evaluation suite stops being a report nobody reads and starts being a gate. Above the threshold, the build passes. Below it, the build fails — the same way a broken unit test already would.

show.event: question card: 'above or below the threshold?'
two outcomes: build passes / build fails

data.question: Is the aggregate above the threshold?

branches.label: Below threshold
branches.fix: build fails, like a broken unit test

resolver.label: The suite is a gate now

beats.narration_text: Every run publishes its report as a build artifact, not a chat message — attached to the commit, kept alongside the ones before it, so a regression shows up as a trend line, not a surprise six weeks later.

show.event: chip reveal: 'chat message' struck through, 'build artifact, per commit' lands

props.sparkLine: A trend line, not a surprise.
props.caption: a regression is a trend line, not a surprise

beats.narration_text: One honest closing boundary: the judge is still a model, grading with the same kind of judgment it's being used to grade. Zheng's own team checked their judge's verdicts against real human preference before trusting it — periodic human spot-checks aren't optional overhead. They're the only check on the checker.

show.event: spark line breathing beat: 'the only check on the checker'

items: the judge is still a model
human spot-checks stay in the loop
props.caption: per Zheng et al.'s own validation against human preference

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A test case is a structured object — input, candidate, reference, rubric — and the judge prompt names its role, states the rubric, and forces a parseable answer. Output parsing should extract a schema, not scrape a sentence, and the three documented biases — position, verbosity, self-enhancement — get bounded by swapping answer order and averaging, not eliminated. A pluggable metric abstraction lets one batch runner — with caching, retries, and concurrency — score any rubric without rewriting the pipeline underneath it. And aggregation compares this run against the last known-good baseline, so wiring that comparison into CI turns the eval suite into a gate a broken model can't quietly pass.

show.event: four artifact lines stagger in, one per act

Output parsing should extract a schema, not scrape a sentence; the three documented biases (position, verbosity, self-enhancement) get bounded by swapping answer order, not eliminated.
A pluggable metric abstraction lets one batch runner — with caching, retries, and concurrency — score any rubric without rewriting the pipeline underneath it.
Aggregation compares this run against the last known-good baseline; wiring that comparison into CI turns the eval suite into a gate, not a report nobody reads.

beats.narration_text: Your turn — here's the prompt, read it with me. 'Design a minimal LLM-as-a-judge harness for one thing I actually ship: name the test case schema, the judge prompt's four required parts, how you'll mitigate position bias specifically, and the one metric your CI pipeline should gate on first.' That last clause matters — pick ONE metric to gate on before you build ten. Run it. Liam, in for Bear.
